questions.title: What normalisation is
questions.text: What is **normalisation**?

options.content: Making a backup copy of every table
Organising data into well-structured related tables so that each fact is stored once and anomalies are avoided
Sorting the records of a table into alphabetical order
Encrypting the data so it cannot be read

scheme.explanation: Normalisation reorganises data into tables following the normal forms to reduce redundancy.

questions.title: Redundancy
questions.text: Data redundancy means that the same data is stored more than once in a database.

scheme.explanation: Redundant copies waste space and can become inconsistent.

questions.title: Benefits of normalisation
questions.text: Select **three** benefits of normalising a database.

options.content: Each fact is stored once, so there is less redundant data
Queries never need to join tables
Changing a fact in one place keeps the data consistent
The database no longer needs primary keys
Update, insertion and deletion anomalies are avoided
Every table has only one field

scheme.mark_scheme: A and C and E. One mark each; a mark is lost for each incorrect option selected.

questions.title: Normalisation and anomalies
questions.text:
A cinema stores all its bookings in one table:

`Bookings(BookingID, ShowDate, FilmTitle, FilmLength, CustomerName, CustomerPhone, Seats)`

A customer who books ten times has their phone number stored ten times. `Seats` holds values such as `"F4, F5, F6"`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- organising data into (related) tables / following normal forms (1)
- so that redundancy is reduced / each fact stored once / anomalies avoided (1)
scheme.model_answer: Normalisation is organising the data of a relational database into well-structured related tables, following the normal forms, so that each fact is stored once and anomalies are avoided.

parts.title: Update anomaly
parts.text: Describe an **update anomaly** that could happen in the `Bookings` table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- customer changes phone number / film length corrected: must be changed in every booking row (1)
- if one row is missed the data becomes inconsistent / two different values for one customer (1)
scheme.model_answer: If a customer changes their phone number, it must be updated in all ten of their bookings; if one row is missed, the table holds two different phone numbers for the same customer.

parts.title: Deletion anomaly
parts.text: Explain why deleting a booking could cause a **deletion anomaly**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- if it is the only booking of a customer / the only showing of a film (1)
- the customer's name and phone / the film's details are lost as well (1)

points.criterion: Only booking of a customer / film

scheme.model_answer: If the booking is the only one for that customer, deleting it also deletes the customer's name and phone number, which the cinema still wanted to keep.

parts.title: Not 1NF
parts.text: Explain why the `Bookings` table is **not** in first normal form.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the field Seats (1)
- holds several values / is not atomic / is a repeating group (1)
scheme.model_answer: The field Seats is not atomic: one cell holds several seat numbers such as F4, F5, F6.

questions.title: The rules of the normal forms
questions.text: A developer is checking the design of a school database against the rules of the normal forms.

parts.title: Rule of 2NF
parts.text: State the rule for **second normal form**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the table is in 1NF (1)
- every non-key field depends on the whole primary key / no partial dependencies (1)
scheme.model_answer: The table is in 1NF and every non-key field depends on the whole primary key, so there are no partial dependencies.

parts.title: Rule of 3NF
parts.text: State the rule for **third normal form**.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the table is in 2NF (1)
- no non-key field depends on another non-key field / no transitive dependencies (1)
scheme.model_answer: The table is in 2NF and no non-key field depends on another non-key field (no transitive dependencies).

parts.title: Single-field key
parts.text: The table `Rooms(RoomNo, Floor, Capacity)` is in 1NF and has the primary key `RoomNo`. Explain why it must also be in 2NF.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- partial dependency means depending on part of a composite key (1)
- RoomNo is a single field so there is no part of the key to depend on (1)
scheme.model_answer: A partial dependency is a dependency on only part of a composite key. RoomNo is a single field, so no field can depend on part of it, and the table is in 2NF.

parts.title: Benefits
parts.text: Give **two** benefits of normalising the school database.

scheme.mark_scheme: Any two (1 each): less redundancy / storage; consistent data / integrity — change in one place; no update / insertion / deletion anomalies; easier to maintain / extend
scheme.model_answer: Each fact is stored only once, which saves storage, and a change is made in one place, so the data stays consistent.

questions.title: Normalising order data
questions.text:
A stationery shop stores its orders in the table below. The primary key is **(OrderID, ProductID)**.

`OrderLines(OrderID, ProductID, OrderDate, CustomerID, CustomerName, ProductName, UnitPrice, Quantity)`

parts.title: Partial dependency
parts.text: Explain why `OrderLines` is **not** in second normal form. Refer to one field in your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- e.g. ProductName / UnitPrice depends only on ProductID; OrderDate / CustomerID depends only on OrderID (1)
- this is only part of the composite key — a partial dependency (1)

points.criterion: Named field and part of key
Partial dependency / part of composite key

scheme.model_answer: ProductName depends only on ProductID, which is only part of the composite key (OrderID, ProductID) — a partial dependency, so the table is not in 2NF.

parts.title: Normalise to 3NF
parts.text: Normalise `OrderLines` to **third normal form**. Write each table in the form `TableName(Field1, Field2, …)`, underline or name the primary key of each table and mark the foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Products(ProductID, ProductName, UnitPrice) with PK ProductID (1)
- Customers(CustomerID, CustomerName) with PK CustomerID (1)
- Orders(OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID) with PK OrderID (1)
- CustomerID in Orders identified as FK (1)
- OrderLines(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity) with composite PK (OrderID, ProductID) (1)
- OrderID and ProductID in OrderLines identified as FKs (1)
Allow equivalent table names. No mark for a table that loses a field.

points.criterion: OrderLines with composite PK and Quantity

scheme.model_answer:
Products(ProductID, ProductName, UnitPrice) — PK ProductID
Customers(CustomerID, CustomerName) — PK CustomerID
Orders(OrderID, OrderDate, CustomerID*) — PK OrderID
OrderLines(OrderID*, ProductID*, Quantity) — PK (OrderID, ProductID)

questions.title: Transitive dependencies
questions.text:
A college stores course data in the table below. The primary key is `CourseID`.

| CourseID | CourseName | TutorID | TutorName | TutorRoom |
|---|---|---|---|---|
| C10 | Robotics | T3 | A. Sadykova | 204 |
| C11 | Python | T3 | A. Sadykova | 204 |
| C12 | Web design | T5 | B. Omarov | 310 |

parts.title: Highest normal form
parts.text: Identify the highest normal form that the table is in and justify your answer.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- 2NF (1)
- single-field key so no partial dependency, but TutorName / TutorRoom depend on TutorID (a non-key field) so it is not 3NF (1)
scheme.model_answer: 2NF: the key CourseID is a single field so there are no partial dependencies, but TutorName and TutorRoom depend on TutorID, a non-key field, so it is not in 3NF.

parts.title: Transitive dependency
parts.text: Describe the **transitive dependency** in this table.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- TutorName / TutorRoom depend on TutorID (1)
- TutorID is a non-key field, which depends on CourseID (CourseID → TutorID → TutorRoom) (1)

points.criterion: TutorID is non-key / chain via key

scheme.model_answer: TutorRoom depends on TutorID, and TutorID depends on the key CourseID, so CourseID → TutorID → TutorRoom: a non-key field depends on another non-key field.

parts.title: Tables in 3NF
parts.text: Normalise the table to **third normal form**. Show the primary and foreign keys.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Tutors(TutorID, TutorName, TutorRoom) with PK TutorID (1)
- Courses(CourseID, CourseName, TutorID) with PK CourseID (1)
- TutorID in Courses is a foreign key (1)
scheme.model_answer: Tutors(TutorID, TutorName, TutorRoom) — PK TutorID; Courses(CourseID, CourseName, TutorID*) — PK CourseID, TutorID is a foreign key.

parts.title: Effect on update
parts.text: A. Sadykova moves to room 215. Explain how the 3NF design makes this change easier.

scheme.mark_scheme: - the room is stored once in Tutors, so only one record is changed (and it cannot become inconsistent) (1)
scheme.model_answer: Her room is stored once in the Tutors table, so only one record needs to be changed.

questions.title: Creating the database
questions.text:
The college creates its normalised database with the tables

`Tutors(TutorID, TutorName, TutorRoom)` and `Courses(CourseID, CourseName, TutorID)`.

`TutorID` is text such as `T3`; `CourseID` is text such as `C10`.

parts.title: Create Courses
parts.text: Write the SQL statement to create the table `Courses` with suitable data types, its primary key and the foreign key that links it to `Tutors`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- CREATE TABLE Courses ( … ) with all three fields (1)
- suitable types, e.g. VARCHAR for CourseID, CourseName, TutorID (1)
- CourseID PRIMARY KEY (1)
- TutorID REFERENCES Tutors(TutorID) / FOREIGN KEY (TutorID) REFERENCES Tutors(TutorID) (1)

parts.title: Order of creation
parts.text: Explain why the table `Tutors` must be created before the table `Courses`.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- Courses.TutorID is a foreign key referring to Tutors (1)
- the referenced table must already exist / referential integrity checks against it (1)
scheme.model_answer: TutorID in Courses is a foreign key that refers to Tutors, so Tutors must already exist for the reference (and referential integrity) to work.

parts.title: Referential integrity
parts.text: A user tries to add a course with `TutorID = 'T9'`, but there is no tutor T9. Explain what happens and why.

scheme.mark_scheme:
- the insert is rejected / error (1)
- referential integrity: a foreign key value must match an existing primary key in Tutors (1)
scheme.model_answer: The insert is rejected because of referential integrity: every TutorID in Courses must match an existing TutorID in Tutors, and T9 does not exist.

summary: Why databases are normalised (redundancy and the update, insertion and deletion anomalies), the rules for first, second and third normal form, how to normalise a table step by step to 3NF, and how to create a database with multiple related tables in SQL.

blocks.content: The process of **organising the data in a relational database into well-structured tables** — by following a set of rules called **normal forms** — so that each fact is stored **once**, data **redundancy** is reduced and **anomalies** (problems when inserting, updating or deleting data) are avoided.

The **same data stored more than once** in a database (for example a customer's address copied into every one of their orders). Redundant data wastes storage and can become **inconsistent** when only some copies are changed.
A **problem that appears when data is inserted, updated or deleted** in a badly designed table: data becomes inconsistent, cannot be added, or is lost by accident.

A customer's address must be changed in every order row
Some data cannot be added without other, unrelated data
A new customer cannot be stored until they place an order
Deleting one record also deletes other important data
Deleting a customer's only order deletes the customer too

items.title: Benefits of normalisation
items.content:
- **Less redundancy** — each fact is stored once, so less storage is used.
- **Consistency / data integrity** — a fact is changed in **one place**, so copies cannot disagree.
- **No anomalies** when inserting, updating or deleting.
- Clearer structure that is easier to **maintain** and extend (add a new table, not new columns).

items.title: Possible drawbacks
items.content:
- More tables, so queries need **joins** — some queries become more complex or slower.
- The design takes more time and skill.
- Very large systems (e.g. reporting databases) sometimes **denormalise** a little for speed.

blocks.title: A school register — spotting the problems
blocks.content:
A school keeps one spreadsheet `Pupils(PupilID, PupilName, Class, ClassTeacher, TeacherRoom)`. 11A has 25 pupils, so **"Mr Omarov, room 204"** is typed 25 times.
- Mr Omarov moves to room 310: the room must be changed **25 times** → update anomaly.
- A new class 11D is created with its teacher, but has no pupils yet: it **cannot be recorded** → insertion anomaly.
- The last pupil of 11C leaves: deleting the pupil also deletes **who teaches 11C** → deletion anomaly.

Normalisation moves the class data into its own table `Classes(Class, ClassTeacher, TeacherRoom)`, so each class's teacher and room are stored **once**.

- Saying normalisation "deletes data" — it **reorganises** data into more tables; no fact is lost.
- Mixing up the anomalies: **update** = change many copies, **insertion** = cannot add, **deletion** = lose other data.
- Writing "it makes the database faster" as the main benefit — the main benefits are **less redundancy** and **consistent data**.

blocks.title: First, second and third normal form
rows: Every field contains **atomic (single) values**; there are **no repeating groups**; each record is **unique** (has a primary key)
One value per cell; no lists; no columns like `Phone1, Phone2, Phone3`
In **1NF**, and every non-key field depends on the **whole** primary key — **no partial dependencies**
Only matters when the primary key is **composite**: a field must not depend on just part of the key
In **2NF**, and **no non-key field depends on another non-key field** — **no transitive dependencies**
"Every non-key field depends on **the key, the whole key and nothing but the key**"

blocks.content: A value that **cannot be split** into smaller meaningful parts for this database — one value per cell. `"Chess, Robotics"` is not atomic; `"Chess"` is.
A **set of fields or values that repeats** for one record, e.g. columns `Club1, Club2, Club3` or a list of values in one cell.
A **primary key made of two or more fields** that together identify a record, e.g. `(StudentID, SubjectID)` in a `Marks` table.
Field B **depends on** field A (written A → B) if each value of A determines **exactly one** value of B. Example: `StudentID → StudentName` (knowing the ID tells you the name).

blocks.title: Types of dependency
rows: A non-key field depends on the **whole** (composite) key
A non-key field depends on **part** of a composite key
`StudentID → StudentName` in a table with key `(StudentID, SubjectID)`
A non-key field depends on **another non-key field**

blocks.content: A partial dependency needs a key with **two or more fields**. So a table in 1NF whose primary key is a **single field** is **automatically in 2NF** — go straight to checking for transitive dependencies.

- Stating the 2NF rule without "**in 1NF**" and the 3NF rule without "**in 2NF**" — each form builds on the previous one.
- Calling a dependency on another non-key field "partial" — that is **transitive** (3NF); **partial** is about **part of a composite key** (2NF).
- Saying 1NF only means "no empty cells" — it means **atomic values, no repeating groups, a primary key**.

theory.title: Exam practice: why normalise and the rules

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: Define the term normalisation. [2]**
Organising the data of a relational database into (well-structured, related) tables (1) so that data redundancy is reduced / each fact is stored once and anomalies are avoided (1).

**Q: List the rules for first normal form. [2]**
All values are atomic / one value per field (1); there are no repeating groups and each record has a (unique) primary key (1).

**Q: State the rule for third normal form. [2]**
The table is in 2NF (1) and no non-key field depends on another non-key field / there are no transitive dependencies (1).

**Q: A table `Orders(OrderID, CustomerName, CustomerAddress, Product)` stores a customer's address in every order. Describe one update anomaly in this table. [2]**
If the customer changes address, the address must be changed in every one of their orders (1); if one row is missed, the table holds two different addresses for the same customer / the data becomes inconsistent (1).

**Q: Explain why a table in 1NF with a single-field primary key is already in 2NF. [2]**
2NF removes partial dependencies, where a field depends on only part of a composite key (1); with a single-field key there is no "part" of the key, so no partial dependency can exist (1).

- Giving the rule for the wrong normal form — learn them in order: **atomic → whole key → nothing but the key**.
- Naming an anomaly without describing **what goes wrong** with an example from the table in the question.
- Writing "duplicate data" without explaining the consequence (**inconsistency**, wasted storage).

items: Define normalisation, redundancy and anomaly.
Describe the update, insertion and deletion anomalies with one example each.
State two benefits and one drawback of normalisation.
State the rules of 1NF, 2NF and 3NF in order.
Explain full, partial and transitive dependency with an example of each.
Explain why a single-field key means a 1NF table is in 2NF.

blocks.title: Converting to 1NF
items: Make every field **atomic**: one value per cell (split multi-value fields; split `FullName` into `FirstName` and `Surname` if needed).
Remove **repeating groups** (columns such as `Country1, Country2…`) — one row per value instead.
Choose a **primary key** so each record is unique — often a **composite** key after splitting.

blocks.title: The same data in 1NF — one row per film–country pair
blocks.content:
| MovieID | Title | Year | Country |
|---|---|---|---|
| M1 | The Nomad | 2005 | Kazakhstan |
| M1 | The Nomad | 2005 | France |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Kazakhstan |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Germany |
| M2 | Tulpan | 2008 | Russia |

Primary key: **(MovieID, Country)**. The table is now in 1NF, but `Title` and `Year` are **repeated** — they depend only on `MovieID`, which is **part** of the key → not yet 2NF.
If a field mixes two kinds of information, such as `Address = "Kazakhstan, Almaty"`, split it into **two atomic fields** `Country` and `City`.

blocks.title: Converting from 1NF to 2NF
items: Identify the **primary key**. If it is a **single field**, a table in 1NF is **already in 2NF**.
If the key is **composite**, check each non-key field: does it depend on the **whole** key or only **part** of it?
Move every field that depends on **only part** of the key into a **new table**, with that part of the key as its primary key.
Keep the part of the key in the original table as a **foreign key**.

blocks.title: 2NF in a shop — order lines
blocks.content:
`OrderLines(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity, ProductName, Price)` with key **(OrderID, ProductID)**:
- `Quantity` depends on the **whole** key (how many of *this* product in *this* order) → stays.
- `ProductName` and `Price` depend only on `ProductID` → **partial dependencies** → move to `Products(ProductID, ProductName, Price)`.

Result: `OrderLines(_OrderID_, _ProductID*_, Quantity)` and `Products(_ProductID_, ProductName, Price)`.

blocks.title: Converting from 2NF to 3NF
items: Look for a **non-key field that depends on another non-key field** (a transitive dependency).
Move those fields into a **new table**; the field they depend on becomes the **primary key** of the new table.
Leave that field in the original table as a **foreign key**.
Check every table again: each non-key field depends on the key, the whole key and nothing but the key.

blocks.title: What each step removes
columns: New key in the new table
rows: Lists in a cell, repeating columns
One value per cell, one row per value
A field that depends on **part** of a composite key
Move it with that part of the key
A non-key field that depends on **another non-key field**

That non-key field (or a new ID)

blocks.content:
- Forgetting to leave a **foreign key** behind when moving fields to a new table — the tables can no longer be linked.
- Moving the field that others depend on **out** of the original table instead of copying it as a foreign key.
- Splitting tables so much that data is **lost** — every original fact must still be stored somewhere.
- Using a name such as `TeacherName` as a key when two teachers could share a name — add an ID such as `TeacherID`.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: `Movies(MovieID, Title, Year, Country)` stores "Kazakhstan, France" in Country. Explain why the table is not in first normal form. [1]**
The field **Country** is **not atomic** — it holds several values in one cell (1). *(Name the field.)*

**Q: `OrderLines(OrderID, ProductID, Quantity, ProductName)` has the key (OrderID, ProductID). Explain why it is not in 2NF. [2]**
ProductName depends only on ProductID (1), which is only part of the composite key — a partial dependency (1).

**Q: Normalise `Courses(CourseID, CourseName, TeacherName, TeacherDOB)` to third normal form. [3]**
`Teachers(TeacherID, TeacherName, TeacherDOB)` with primary key TeacherID (1); `Courses(CourseID, CourseName, TeacherID)` with primary key CourseID (1); TeacherID in Courses is a foreign key linking the tables (1).

**Q: State what happens to the field a transitive dependency depends on. [2]**
It becomes the primary key of the new table (1) and stays in the original table as a foreign key (1).

- Writing table designs without marking the **primary key** (underline) and the **foreign key** (asterisk) — marks are given for them.
- Normalising to 3NF but losing a field from the original table.
- Explaining "not 2NF" without naming **which** field depends on **which part** of the key.

blocks.title: Another scenario — a clinic
blocks.content:
Unnormalised: `Visits(VisitID, VisitDate, PatientID, PatientName, PatientPhone, DoctorID, DoctorName, Room, Treatments)` where `Treatments` lists several treatments.
1. **1NF**: one row per treatment → key **(VisitID, Treatment)**.
2. **2NF**: everything except the treatment depends on `VisitID` only → `Visits(VisitID, VisitDate, PatientID, PatientName, PatientPhone, DoctorID, DoctorName, Room)` and `VisitTreatments(VisitID*, Treatment)`.
3. **3NF**: `PatientName, PatientPhone` depend on `PatientID`; `DoctorName, Room` depend on `DoctorID` → `Patients(PatientID, PatientName, PatientPhone)`, `Doctors(DoctorID, DoctorName, Room)`, `Visits(VisitID, VisitDate, PatientID*, DoctorID*)`, `VisitTreatments(VisitID*, Treatment)`.

blocks.title: From the normalised design to a working database
items: Create a table for each table in the 3NF design, with the correct **data types** (from the data dictionary).
Set each table's **primary key** (composite where needed).
Create the **foreign keys** (`REFERENCES`) — the relationships between tables, with **referential integrity**.
Create the tables in the right order: the **"one" side first** (e.g. `Classes`), then the tables that refer to it.
Enter test data — first in the "one" tables, then in the "many" tables.
Test with **queries** that join the tables.

blocks.content: A rule that **every foreign key value must match an existing primary key value** in the related table. The DBMS rejects, for example, a pupil in class `11Z` if there is no class `11Z` in `Classes`.

blocks.caption: Creating the normalised tables in SQL

blocks.content:
- Giving a foreign key a **different data type or size** from the primary key it refers to — they must match.
- Creating `Pupils` before `Classes` — the foreign key refers to a table that does not exist yet.
- Inserting a pupil with a class that is not in `Classes` — rejected by **referential integrity**.
- Writing two `PRIMARY KEY` words for a composite key — use **one** `PRIMARY KEY (a, b)`.

blocks.title: Exam-style answers
blocks.content:
**Q: A library stores `Loans(LoanID, BookID, Title, Author, PupilID, PupilName, LoanDate)`. Normalise it to 3NF. [4]**
`Books(BookID, Title, Author)` with key BookID (1); `Pupils(PupilID, PupilName)` with key PupilID (1); `Loans(LoanID, BookID*, PupilID*, LoanDate)` with key LoanID (1); BookID and PupilID in Loans are foreign keys (1).

**Q: Write SQL to create the table `Memberships` with a composite primary key made of the foreign keys PupilID and ClubID. [3]**
`CREATE TABLE Memberships (PupilID VARCHAR(5) REFERENCES Pupils(PupilID), ClubID INTEGER REFERENCES Clubs(ClubID), PRIMARY KEY (PupilID, ClubID));` — CREATE TABLE with both fields and types (1); both REFERENCES (1); PRIMARY KEY (PupilID, ClubID) (1).

**Q: Explain why the table `Classes` must be created before `Pupils`. [2]**
`Pupils.Class` is a foreign key that refers to `Classes` (1); the table it refers to must exist (and contain the class) before pupils can be linked to it / for referential integrity (1).

**Q: Explain what is meant by referential integrity. [2]**
Every foreign key value must match a primary key value in the related table (1), so a record cannot refer to a record that does not exist (1).

- Saying a table is "not in 1NF" without naming the **field** and the problem.
- Thinking 2NF matters for single-field keys — a 1NF table with a **single-field key** is automatically in 2NF.
- Forgetting to leave a **foreign key** behind when moving fields to a new table.
- Confusing a **partial** dependency (2NF) with a **transitive** one (3NF).
- Writing SQL with a foreign key whose type does not match the primary key.
